81: Class weighting changes how strongly errors on a target class influence the training loss.
Collecting and labeling more examples takes time, while the question asks for a quick change to the existing model.
An anomaly detector changes the task and model, rather than directly improving target-class recall in the current classifier.
Switching algorithms requires new tuning and does not automatically correct the target class's insufficient loss contribution.
Increasing the target class's weight penalizes its misclassification more strongly, directly encouraging better recall with a small training change.

Streaming describes how records arrive and are served, not the number or type of target labels.
Each transaction is fraudulent or not fraudulent; the model can return the estimated probability of the fraudulent class.
Multiclass classification requires more than two target categories, which are not specified here.
A probability-valued classifier output does not turn the fraud/no-fraud target into an ordinary regression task.

84: Perfectly dependent columns cause rank deficiency and non-unique ordinary least-squares coefficients.
Ordinary least squares does not require neural-network backpropagation; rank deficiency is the relevant mathematical issue.
The normal-equation matrix becomes singular, so a unique coefficient vector cannot be recovered by ordinary inversion without additional constraints.
Feature dependence does not change the definition of the least-squares loss; it creates multiple coefficient solutions with the same fitted values.
The relationship described is exactly linear, not evidence that nonlinear dependencies were introduced.

86: SageMaker launches a training container with a train argument, so its entrypoint must start or dispatch the training program.
A shell profile is not a reliable container startup mechanism because the training launch does not require an interactive login shell.
SageMaker supplies its training command and can override CMD; relying only on CMD does not define the required training entrypoint behavior.
Use an ENTRYPOINT that launches training or handles the train argument. The executable need not literally be named train; handling the launch contract is what matters.
Copying a program into /opt/ml/train does not configure Docker to execute it or handle SageMaker's training argument.
87: Transformations can reduce the influence of right-skewed numeric features; non-normality alone does not necessarily indicate bad data.
Cross-validation evaluates generalization and does not transform feature distributions.
Binning represents values by ranges, reducing sensitivity to extreme magnitudes when that representation is useful for the model.
High-degree polynomial terms can magnify large values and worsen the effect of an already long right tail.
A logarithmic transform compresses large positive values and can reduce right skew; zeros and negative values require appropriate handling.
One-hot encoding represents categories and is not, by itself, a transformation that corrects a continuous distribution's skew.
88: Regularization targets a model that fits training data much better than held-out data.
Shuffling improves batch composition, but does not directly constrain the excess fitting capacity causing the generalization gap.
The dataset is already large; reallocating held-out observations may weaken evaluation and does not directly regularize the model.
L1/L2 penalties and dropout constrain memorization while preserving the architecture, addressing the stated overfitting directly.
Reducing capacity can also help, but may discard useful representation. It is an alternative to validate, rather than proof of the highest accuracy from the supplied information.
89: A low-dimensional scatter plot can reveal local neighborhoods in a high-dimensional feature representation.
t-SNE maps numerical feature vectors into a low-dimensional layout that can be inspected for visible groups; such groups still need validation.
An elbow plot helps choose a k-means cluster count but does not show the individual observations' neighborhood structure.
A line graph suggests an ordering and connections between observations that the embedding does not define.
Many per-feature box plots require more analysis and do not provide a single direct view of the high-dimensional grouping structure.
90: Interruptible capacity is safest for replaceable EMR compute that does not hold the cluster's persistent HDFS data.
Interrupting the single primary/master node threatens cluster coordination and availability.
Core nodes store HDFS blocks as well as execute tasks, so interruption can affect data availability and the long-running cluster.
Task nodes add processing capacity without storing HDFS blocks, making them the preferred Spot tier for this architecture.
Including core nodes increases storage disruption risk; restricting Spot to task nodes better protects the long-running cluster.
91: Predictive maintenance can be supervised by aligning sensor histories with later observed failure events.
Future-fault labels define the prediction target, and an RNN can learn temporal patterns in sensor sequences that precede those failures.
Clustering finds similar behavior but does not directly learn which sequences predict a known future fault.
Temporal CNNs can be valid alternatives, but this option does not specify such a design; the RNN is the direct sequential model offered.
Being a time series does not automatically define a seq2seq target or supply the future-fault labels needed for this maintenance objective.
92: Feature screening for a linear predictor should consider association with its target, not simply feature scale.
High variance can reflect different measurement units or useful signal; it is not evidence that a feature is irrelevant.
Low variance may identify nearly constant fields, but does not generally establish their relationship to the sale-price target.
Low correlation with other predictors can mean a feature provides independent useful information, rather than being irrelevant.
Target correlation provides a simple screen for linear relevance. Validate removals because weak marginal correlation can still hide conditional predictive value.
93: Axis-aligned thresholds can efficiently represent the rectangular class region shown in the plot.
A single linear separating boundary cannot isolate the central rectangle from points surrounding it on all sides.
A decision tree can bound the red region with thresholds on x and y, closely matching its axis-aligned rectangular shape.
An RBF SVM can fit nonlinear boundaries too, but requires kernel tuning; the tree directly matches the rectangular structure. The plot alone cannot guarantee a universal accuracy ranking.
A single perceptron remains a linear separator in these inputs even with tanh activation, so it cannot enclose the rectangle.
94: A very deep network trained on a small image dataset can memorize training examples rather than generalize.
Adding layers increases capacity despite the evidence that the existing model already overfits.
Reducing depth limits capacity and can improve generalization from only 1,000 training images.
A smaller learning rate changes optimization speed; it does not directly remedy the large train–test gap.
Dropout regularizes hidden representations and discourages dependence on training-specific feature combinations.
Using test images in training leaks evaluation information and prevents an honest estimate of generalization.
Early stopping selects a checkpoint before validation performance deteriorates, avoiding additional fitting of training noise.
95: When validation loss rises while training loss falls, later epochs are worsening generalization.
Stop near the best validation-loss checkpoint, before the rise after roughly epoch 60, and restore those weights.
Changing the random seed does not directly address the consistent late-training overfitting pattern in the graph.
More epochs continue the region where validation error is rising, so they are likely to worsen the shown problem.
An extra layer adds capacity when the graph already indicates overfitting rather than insufficient capacity.
96: Heteroscedasticity means that residual variability changes with the predictor or fitted value.
The residual spread grows at higher x values, violating constant-variance assumptions of the basic homoscedastic linear-regression model; a transform or weighted/robust treatment may be needed.
Some residuals are large, but the systematic widening is stronger evidence of nonconstant variance than isolated outliers alone.
Residuals near zero at some locations do not establish that the constant-variance model is appropriate.
The high-x residuals are much more dispersed than low-x residuals, directly contradicting constant variance.

100: Stratified folds preserve representation of a rare class during cross-validation.
Ordinary random folds may contain very few or no positive cases when the disease rate is only 3%.
Stratified five-fold cross-validation distributes the small number of positive cases across folds, making each evaluation more representative.
Repeating unstratified folds does not ensure that the rare class is adequately represented in each fold.
A stratified holdout preserves class proportions but provides only one split; it is not the requested cross-validation approach.
